Can CRISPR screens tell us what unknown human genes do? A pre-registered test

This project, including this explainer, was produced by AI agents and has not been verified by a human. The longer, more detailed explainer is in ../explainer/; the paper is manuscript/manuscript.md.

In one paragraph. Thousands of human genes have no known function. This project took a published idea, that genes whose loss harms the same cancer cell lines probably work together, and tested it strictly. The gene list was fixed before any analysis. The method was scored on genes whose function was discovered after 2018. Literature judges saw decoy statements next to the real ones. The answer: the method beats chance but rarely names the exact function. It does far worse than reading the gene's existing computer-predicted annotations, and most of its best predictions concern genes whose function was already published.

1. The problem

Thousands of human genes have no recorded function, and the databases lag behind the literature.

About one human protein-coding gene in four (4,924 of 19,296) has no experimentally supported function in the Gene Ontology (GO, the standard database of gene functions), and either a low score in the UniProt protein database or little focused literature. Research attention is very unequal: known genes attract more papers, and unknown genes stay unknown (Stoeger 2018; Haynes 2018).

Large CRISPR knockout screens could help. The Cancer Dependency Map (DepMap; Tsherniak 2017) switches off each gene, one at a time, in over a thousand cancer cell lines and measures how much each loss slows growth (Dempster 2021). This project used 1,361 cell lines. Every gene therefore has a profile, a list of which cell lines need it. That profile is free information about every gene, studied or not.

2. The idea in 60 seconds

Genes whose loss hurts the same cell lines probably work together. The hard part is not fooling yourself about how often this is right.

If knocking out gene A slows exactly the cell lines that need genes B, C and D, the four probably belong to the same complex or pathway. This is co-essentiality (Pan 2018; Kim 2019; Wainberg 2021). If B, C and D process microRNAs, A probably does too: guilt by association.

The trap is in the checking. The usual test hides a well-studied gene's annotations and sees if its partners recover them ("leave-one-out"). Multifunctional, well-annotated genes are easy to predict this way, so the test flatters the method (Gillis & Pavlidis 2011, 2012). And the famous success stories were often confirmed by papers that themselves used DepMap.

This project's twist is strict testing. It fixed its rules before seeing the answer, as clinical trials do (pre-registration; Nosek 2018). It tested on genes whose functions were discovered later, the design of the CAFA function-prediction challenges (Radivojac 2013). And it checked whether a stated confidence of 10% comes true about 10% of the time. AI agents planned and ran all of it (section 7).

3. The method in five steps

Click a step to jump to it.

We follow one gene throughout: ANKRD52, which came out top of the final shortlist.

Step 1. Pick the genes before looking

The list of "uncharacterised" genes was built from databases alone and locked before any two genes were compared.

  • What. A gene counts if it has no informative GO function backed by experiment ("protein binding" does not count), and either a low UniProt score, few "focused" papers (papers about 10 genes or fewer), or membership of the "dark protein" class of the Illuminating the Druggable Genome programme. This gave 4,924 genes. The list was locked with a digital fingerprint (a hash); every later script refused to run unless it matched. An independent agent rebuilt the list with its own code and got the same genes.
  • Why. Choosing genes after seeing the data drifts towards genes where the method looks good.
  • ANKRD52. Its only experimental GO entries say "protein binding", and only 6 of the 62 papers that mention it are focused, so it is on the list. In fact a 2017 paper had already worked out its function (Golden 2017); the database had never recorded it.

Step 2. Find each gene's partners

Each gene's 25 most co-essential partners come from an existing scoring tool, used unchanged.

  • What. The project brief required a co-essentiality scoring tool published in the cancergenetics GitHub organisation by the Ryan lab at University College Dublin (itself built by AI agents during a hackathon): github.com/cancergenetics/ai-hackathon-Coessentiality. It scores every gene pair by combining three views: how similar the two profiles are once screen-wide patterns are removed, how much the genes' own partner lists overlap, and how close they sit in a map of the whole network. The agents first checked that it reproduced its published benchmark; it did. Partners on the same chromosome arm, and close relatives by gene duplication (paralogues), are removed: CRISPR cutting can make neighbouring genes look co-essential for reasons unrelated to function (Lazar 2024).
  • Why. The partner list is the only evidence the method uses.
  • ANKRD52. Its top partners are AGO2, XPO5, DICER1, DROSHA, TNRC6A, DGCR8 and TNRC6B: the core microRNA machinery. Eighth is PPP6C, the phosphatase ANKRD52 is known to bind. The exclusion also discarded one true partner (TARBP2, a Dicer helper on the same chromosome arm), so the guard has a cost.

Step 3. Keep only genes whose partner list is reproducible

If a gene's partners change when you use a different half of the cell lines, they are noise, and the gene is flagged.

  • What. The cell lines are split into two halves, five times, and each half gives a top-25 list. The overlap is compared with what 200 look-alike genes achieve. Look-alikes are genes whose profiles have similar overall strength, spread and missing data; any overlap they show is chance. (The same idea is reused later as a chance baseline for accuracy.) A gene passes if it beats its look-alikes and is expressed in the cells. Genes that fail still get a prediction, but it is flagged and cannot enter the shortlist.
  • Why. Many unknown genes are barely expressed or never needed, often because a paralogue covers for them (Dede 2020). Their profiles are flat, and their "partners" arbitrary.
  • ANKRD52. The halves shared about 12 of 25 partners; look-alikes shared almost none. It clearly passes.

Only 646 of 4,924 genes (13%) passed. The check leaks: genes that are not expressed at all, used as a negative control, passed the reproducibility part 13% of the time, not the planned 5%. Allowing for this, at least about 320 genes, roughly 1 in 15 of the list, carry a real signal. That figure assumes the leak rate seen in non-expressed genes also applies to expressed ones, which was not tested.

Step 4. Guess a function and say how sure

Partners vote for GO terms, weighted by link strength; a probability learned from later discoveries says how much to trust the winner.

  • The guess. For each GO term, add up the scores of the partners annotated to it. The top term with at least two supporting partners wins. Of three rules declared in advance, the simplest won a fixed contest.
  • The confidence. A simple statistical model (logistic regression) turns a few facts into a probability: mainly how strong the partners are, how many of them carry any annotation, and the kind of term. (Term size was also offered to the model but got zero weight.) It was fitted on the 2018 test set of Step 5, so it is calibrated: of guesses given 10%, about 10% should come true. Only genes that resemble the test set get one (2,583 genes).
  • Why. Confidence learned the usual way, on well-studied genes, promised about three times more hits than were delivered (section 5).
  • ANKRD52. Eight partners vote for "regulatory ncRNA-mediated gene silencing", the microRNA pathway. Its confidence is 0.14, about 1 in 7, the highest of all 2,583 genes. In plain words: if ANKRD52 gains any new experimental annotation in the next 8 years or so, there is about a 1 in 7 chance it will be exactly this term. The vote also missed something: ANKRD52's biochemical home, the PP6 phosphatase, ranks only 37th, because few PP6 members have experimental GO terms. The vote follows the best-annotated partners.

Keeping the gene sets straight. 4,271 of the 4,924 genes can be measured by the tool. 646 pass the reproducibility check. 2,583 resemble the 2018 test genes closely enough to get a confidence value. Only 269 are in both groups; the shortlist was drawn from these, and the top 40 are the 40 with the highest confidence. Genes that fail the reproducibility check still get a confidence value if they resemble the test genes, which is why most of the "expected confirmations" in section 5 come from flagged genes (Fine print).

Step 5. Test the guesses honestly

Three tests: genes annotated after 2018, blinded literature judges with decoys, and data that never saw DepMap.

  • The 2018 test set. GO was rolled back to 2 July 2018. The test genes were "uncharacterised" by the same rule then and have gained experimental annotations since: 809 genes. The method predicted from 2018 annotations and was scored against what curators added later. Annotations from papers that used DepMap were removed first, so the method could not be "confirmed" by its own data source. The test was written down half an hour before the data were opened, and that pre-registered look was taken once.
  • Blinded literature check. One agent collected literature on each top gene without seeing any prediction. Two judge agents then saw that evidence, gene name hidden, next to four statements: the real prediction and three decoys (other genes' predictions from a similar family of terms and of similar size). The judges were first validated on genes with known answers.
  • Independent data. Protein interaction, protein co-abundance, localisation, single-cell perturbation and predicted-structure data were checked for whether they place the gene near its predicted partners.
  • ANKRD52. Both judges supported the real statement and none of the decoys. It is correct but already published: ANKRD52's phosphatase removes phosphates from AGO2 in a cycle needed for microRNA silencing (Golden 2017), and earlier co-essentiality catalogues had linked it to this machinery (Kim 2019; Wainberg 2021).

Where the genes went

4. Following one gene: ANKRD52 start to finish

The method works as intended on ANKRD52, but the answer was already in the literature.

This is the typical story of the method's best predictions. It is good at recognising genes inside well-defined machinery. Those are exactly the genes experimentalists have often already characterised, even when the databases have not caught up.

5. Did it work? A scorecard

Better than chance but modest; the confidence numbers are not detectably off but rest on only 24 correct guesses; the literature agrees far more than for decoys, mostly because many "unknown" genes were already known.

Test 1: predicting functions discovered after 2018. Verdict: passes, but weak. All 809 test genes are, by construction, genes that did gain an annotation. So the result reads: among unknown genes that later get annotated, the top guess matches the new annotation for 3%, about 1 in 30, against 0.5% for look-alike genes. But:

  • It is no better than an older co-essentiality score (GLS, a correlation corrected for related cell lines; Wainberg 2021), at 2.3%. The tool's lead at finding protein-complex partners did not carry over to function.
  • It is far below homology: 22%, about 1 in 5. Here "homology" means ranking the GO terms the gene already had in 2018 from computer predictions (based on sequence similarity, protein domains and evolutionary trees). These do not count as experimental evidence, which is why "uncharacterised" genes can have them. Homology makes a guess for only 57% of the test genes, yet still wins.
  • Where the signal is strong it does better: about 1 in 8 (12%) in the fifth of genes with the strongest partners, never in the weakest two-fifths, and 18% for membership of a protein complex.

Test 2: are the confidence numbers honest? Verdict: not detectably off, but thin and low. On the 2018 test set the average predicted and observed hit rates agree (3.1% each), and the finer checks show no clear miscalibration. But the model rests on only 24 correct guesses. A model learned on well-studied genes would have promised 8.9%. The highest confidence for any gene is 0.14; the bars set in advance for "confident" (0.3 and 0.5) were never reached. Because confidence is conditional on later annotation, about 30 top guesses would be confirmed if every calibrated gene were annotated. Only about 1 in 6 such genes gains annotation in 8 years, so the realistic expectation is about 5 confirmations out of 2,583 genes.

Test 3: does the literature agree? Verdict: far more than for decoys, but mostly with what was already known. Judges supported 18 of the top 40 predictions (45%) against 3 of 120 decoys (2.5%), after passing a check on known genes (9 of 10 real statements, 1 of 30 decoys). Support fell with rank: 12 of the top 20, 6 of the next 20, and 1 of 30 lower-confidence genes. (A separate list of 20 strong-signal genes too unusual to calibrate scored 19 of 20.) The independent data barely separated real predictions from fake ones (32% versus 28% for look-alike genes and 22% for decoys), so they were reported but never used to rank.

Already known, three ways. Of the top 40 genes, the blind literature agent found that 31 already had a published function. The judges supported the prediction for 16 of those 31, plus 2 others: the 18. For the other 15, the judges found the predicted term not addressed, or contradicted. Separately, 34 of 40 genes already had a published link to one of their top partners in earlier co-essentiality or protein-interaction catalogues, though not necessarily with the same function. Only 3 of 40 had been explicitly predicted before (Wainberg 2021).

What this does not show.

  • It is not a discovery list: most top genes were already characterised, and only 2 of the 18 supported predictions concern genes whose function was not already established.
  • The confidence applies only if a gene gets annotated at all, and rests on 24 correct guesses.
  • The 2018 test genes have stronger signals than today's unknown genes; reweighted to resemble them, accuracy falls to about 1%.
  • The literature test is easy to pass (decoys are other genes' terms), and both judges were the same AI model.
  • Nothing was tested at the bench, and no human has checked any result.

6. Five things we learned

Ranked by how much they should change what you do; the surprising ones first.

  1. "Uncharacterised" in a database often means "not yet curated", not "unstudied". In a random 50 of the list, an audit agent found that 42% already had an experimentally established function. Part of the cause is mechanical: counting only "focused" papers makes complex subunits look unstudied, because they are described in papers about the whole complex (288 listed genes are curated complex subunits). Check the literature, not just the databases.
  2. Most unknown genes are invisible to co-essentiality. At least 1 in 15 carries a real signal. Olfactory and skin gene families are almost entirely silent (2 of 516 passed), mostly because they are not expressed in these cell lines. A method should say "no information" for most genes.
  3. Homology beats co-essentiality about seven to one at predicting future annotations. They are partly complementary (15 of co-essentiality's 24 correct guesses were missed by homology), but using co-essentiality only where homology is silent adds just 0.6 percentage points. Use homology first.
  4. Testing on well-studied genes gives an accuracy about five times higher: 14% with known genes' annotations hidden, 3% on genes annotated after 2018. Part of the gap is information leaking from the known answers; part is that well-studied genes differ (more essential, better connected). Read any leave-one-out-only claim with this in mind.
  5. Most top genes already had a published link to their predicted partners. 34 of the top 40 did; only 3 of 40 had been explicitly predicted before. Of ten genes chosen for detailed write-ups, only PLEKHH3 (a possible brake on PI3K/AKT signalling, linked to PTEN) had no precedent anywhere checked.

7. How the AI team got here

One rule shaped the method: fix the rule before seeing the answer, then check it on genes discovered later. Each time a claim met a stricter check, it shrank.

The research took about 15 hours (29 to 30 October 2026, UTC). Six moments mattered most.

  1. Test on the future (20:06–20:18). Question: how do we know a prediction is right? Evidence: the literature review flagged leave-one-out's bias and proposed a time-split test; reviewer agents then noted that success stories were confirmed by DepMap-based papers (18 of 19 later annotations for SLC25A51). Decision: score on genes annotated after 2018, minus DepMap-derived annotations.
  2. Freeze the list first (21:00). Question: what does "uncharacterised" mean? Evidence: no single measure of "known-ness" suffices (Stoeger 2018; Oprea 2018; Rocha 2023). Decision: combine four measures and lock the list. Sixteen minutes later an audit found 42% of a sample already known; as pre-registered, no gene was removed.
  3. Flag silent genes (21:55). Question: which genes can the method speak about? Evidence: a statistics reviewer agent said the first rule (keep the most reproducible 5%) was a cut-off, not a test against chance. Decision: compare each gene with 200 look-alikes, with non-expressed genes as a control. That control showed the 13% false-pass rate.
  4. One look at the test set (22:50). Question: how good is it? Evidence: the simplest voting rule won on known genes; the single look at the 2018 test set gave 3%, tied with the older score, far behind homology. An independent agent re-derived it gene by gene. Decision: frame the method as a weak signal, not an annotator.
  5. Nobody clears the bar (04:55). Question: which predictions make the shortlist? Evidence: no gene reached the confidence tiers; extra robustness checks (repeat without the most dependent cancer type, in RNA-interference screens, and test for TP53 dependence) failed 221 of 269 candidates and had never been tried on known positives. Decision: rank by confidence alone and show failed checks as labels. The principal-investigator (PI) agent also kept a separate list for "machinery" genes (mitochondria, ribosome, DNA repair, RNA processing, centrosome), which were too rare in the 2018 test set to calibrate; mitochondrial modules dominate co-essentiality (Rahman 2021).
  6. Referees reframe the claims (07:47–10:26). Question: is the story right? Evidence: two referee agents found that confidence is conditional on later annotation, the signal count included chance passes, the gene definition admitted known complex subunits, and novelty had not been checked against earlier catalogues. Decision: report all four. No pre-specified result changed; the interpretation did.

Who did what. A PI agent (Claude Opus 5.5) designed the study and made every decision. Sub-agents (Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5; about 60 by the PI's estimate, as the run log was not kept) wrote code, reviewed the design, re-derived results, did the blind literature work and judging, and refereed the manuscript. By the PI's account (there is no transcript to check), the human wrote the brief, had the DepMap files on the machine, restarted the run after a usage-limit pause and gave publishing instructions, with no scientific direction.

Where it went in circles. Design reviews produced dozens of quick fixes but missed the big problems that the referees found. Ten candidate reports were written before anyone checked earlier catalogues; nine then needed novelty corrections.

Further caveats.

  • About 82% of the expected confirmations come from genes that fail the reproducibility check. For the 269 reproducible, calibrated genes, about one confirmation is expected (derived for the earlier explainer).
  • Simpler confidence models calibrate equally well but share only 7 to 14 of the top 40 genes: the ranking is fragile.
  • The network is from 2026; only annotations were rolled back to 2018. The tool was tuned on a protein-complex atlas built after 2018. An untuned plain correlation did as well, which limits but does not measure this leak.
  • A judging rule crediting matches to a module label, not logged before judging, moved 16 to 18. Decoys from the same gene's lower-ranked guesses were not tried.
  • Data sources for the independent check were admitted only after recovering known complexes, but the final support rule and the robustness checks were never validated on known positives.
  • Homology's strength may partly reflect curators confirming terms that computer predictions had already suggested (untested).

When not to use it. As a general annotator (use homology or protein-interaction data first). For genes that fail the reproducibility check, about 87% of the list. To claim novelty without checking earlier catalogues (Wainberg 2021; Kim 2019). For machinery genes, which have no calibrated confidence.

9. Glossary
  • Calibrated confidence. A probability that means what it says: of predictions given 10%, about 10% come true.
  • Co-essentiality. Two genes are co-essential when knocking out either harms the same cell lines.
  • CRISPR knockout screen. An experiment that disables genes one by one and measures the effect on cell growth.
  • Decoy. A plausible but wrong statement shown to judges beside the real one, to measure how easily they say "supported".
  • DepMap. The Cancer Dependency Map: genome-wide CRISPR screens in over a thousand cancer cell lines.
  • GLS. An older co-essentiality score: a correlation corrected for related cell lines.
  • GO term. An entry in the Gene Ontology describing a biological process, molecular function or location.
  • Homology baseline. Ranking the computer-predicted GO terms a gene already had in 2018.
  • Leave-one-out. Hiding a known gene's annotations and predicting them back.
  • Look-alike genes. Genes with similar profile strength, spread and missing data, used to measure chance.
  • Machinery genes. Genes predicted to work in core cell machinery (mitochondria, ribosome, DNA repair, RNA processing, centrosome).
  • Paralogue. A related gene arising from gene duplication.
  • Pre-registration. Writing down data, analyses and decision rules before seeing results.
  • Robustness checks. Re-running a prediction without the most dependent cancer type, in RNA-interference screens, and testing for TP53 dependence.
